# Summary {.unnumbered}

We provide estimates of the wood provision ecosystem service for the 27 Member States of the European Union in 2000, 2006,
2012, 2018 and 2024, following the accounting method of INCA Part III [@lanotte2021], which updates INCA Part II
[@vallecillo2019]. The actual flow is the net annual increment of the forest available for wood supply, which is
{{< fact nai_mm3_2000 >}} million cubic metres in 2000 and {{< fact nai_mm3_2024 >}} million cubic metres in 2024. Part of that
change comes from a change of source within the series, as @sec-breaks shows. In 2024, {{< fact n_overuse_2024 >}} Member States
show overuse, adding up to {{< fact overuse_mm3_2024 >}} million cubic metres, and those flags rest on values carried forward from
earlier years. At constant 2010 prices, the actual flow is worth {{< fact value_constant_bn_2000 >}} billion euro in 2000 and
{{< fact value_constant_bn_2024 >}} billion euro in 2024, and the overuse of 2024 is worth {{< fact overuse_constant_meur_2024 >}}
million euro. All quantities are reported by NUTS0, NUTS2 and NUTS3 region and mapped at 100 m.

# Introduction

Wood provision is the ecological contribution to the production of timber that can be harvested and used as a raw material. Its
underlying process is the natural growth of a biotic resource, so the accounts measure it through the net annual increment
(NAI) of standing timber in the forest available for wood supply [@lanotte2021]. NAI is the average annual growth in volume of
living trees less the average annual losses from natural mortality, measured here in cubic metres over bark
[@eurostat2026handbook]. Forest available for wood supply is forest without environmental, social or economic restrictions with a
significant impact on the supply of wood.

Services with a regeneration rate can be used faster than they renew, so the accounts also compare use with regeneration. Overuse
is the part of the use that exceeds regeneration, and the sustainable flow is the part that stays within it. This report describes
how we estimated those quantities and valued them, why we took each decision along the way and what the estimates show.

## Sources of orientation

The method comes from Chapter 4 of INCA Part II and Section 6.2 of INCA Part III, and these reports settle any question they
address. Section 6.2 of Part III replaces two steps of Part II. It reports the whole NAI as the flow, because the forest asset
accounts already record natural growth as an addition to the stock, and because forest management does not change stand volume
growth much within a range of thinning grades [@lanotte2021]. The ecosystem contribution coefficient of Part II is therefore
dropped. It also replaces the valuation through the output of forestry with a valuation through export prices.

The INCA tool applies the same method and adds details that the reports do not state, such as the list of outliers described in
@sec-screen [@incatool]. We took those details from it. The reports give no method for overuse of wood or for the sustainable
flow, so those steps are decisions of this work, explained below.

# Results

## Actual flow

The actual flow of the EU27 is {{< fact nai_mm3_2000 >}} million cubic metres in 2000, {{< fact nai_mm3_2012 >}} million in 2012
and {{< fact nai_mm3_2024 >}} million in 2024 (@tbl-eu). The series mixes model estimates of total forest with reported values of
available forest, so its changes between reporting years should be read with @tbl-sources and @tbl-breaks. @fig-map-nai places the
flow on forest within each country.

::: {#tbl-eu}

Physical accounts of the EU27, in million cubic metres. The last column counts Member States with overuse.
:::

![Actual flow of wood provision, in thousand cubic metres per 10 km cell, shown as the sum of the 1 km cells.](figures/wood_map_nai.png){#fig-map-nai width=100%}

## Sustainable flow and overuse

Removals exceed the increment in {{< fact n_overuse_2024 >}} Member States in 2024 (@tbl-overuse and @fig-ratio). The sustainable
flow equals the removals wherever they stay below the increment, which is the case in every other Member State and year shown.

::: {#tbl-overuse}
{{< datatable overuse_cases >}}

Member States with overuse in the reporting years, in thousand cubic metres.
:::

![Removals divided by the net annual increment, by Member State. Points to the right of the dashed line are overuse. Malta has no values.](figures/wood_removals_to_nai.png){#fig-ratio width=100%}

2024 (@tbl-value). @fig-map-value shows the value at 10 km, and @fig-unit-value the unit value of each Member State with the
origin of its ratio. @tbl-unit-value gives the range of unit values in each reporting year, and @tbl-value-country the value by

# Limitations

**Statistics.** Values reported for available forest cover few countries before 2018, and most values before then are model
estimates of total forest, so they probably overstate the flow. Changes of source move the series for reasons that have nothing to
do with forests, as @tbl-breaks shows, so comparisons over time within those countries need care. The carbon budget series ends in
2019 and is flat from 2016, and the values of 2024 mostly repeat earlier years. They should be refreshed when Eurostat holds more of
that year.

**Overuse.** The removals of available forest are compared with a NAI that in some countries refers to total forest, which
understates overuse in those countries. The ratio could cross the threshold in more countries if the model estimates were scaled to
available forest. Regional overuse is the national overuse shared by the key, so it does not show where overharvesting occurs inside
a country. A map of overuse has the same limit.

**Value.** Few countries report the timber value before 2012, so most early values come from an export price divided by a mean
ratio, and the monetary series is better read as an estimate than as a measurement. {{< fact ratio_eu_mean_2012 >}} Member States
take the EU mean in 2012, of which {{< fact screened_count >}} lost their timber values in the screening, so they all share one
ratio. A country with low export volumes can have an unrepresentative export price. Every cell and region of a country has one unit
value, so the maps do not show price differences within a country.

**Space.** The key combines forest with the productivity of the vegetation, and productivity measures growth of vegetation in
general, so some flow is placed on forest that is not harvested. Productivity comes from a 1 km product in 2000, 2006 and 2012 and
from a 300 m product in 2018 and 2024, so spatial detail differs between the two groups and changes in the pattern between them
partly reflect the change of product. The equivalence of the gross and net products rests on a sample of 10 of the 180 pairs of
files, as the Methods section explains. The Corine accounting layers have a minimum mapping unit of 25 hectares. Regional shares use
weights at 1 km, whose cells on borders are assigned by their centre, so they can differ slightly from a sum of the 100 m maps.
